title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.1 Оршил
Стационар байдал нь хугацааны цувааны шинжилгээний хамгийн чухал ойлголтуудын нэг юм.
Автокорреляцын шинжилгээ, AR загварууд, MA загварууд, ARMA загварууд зэрэг хугацааны цувааны олон статистик арга нь суурь процесс стационар байна гэж үздэг.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.2 Хатуу стационар байдал
\[\{Y_t\}\] стохастик процессийг хатуу стационар гэнэ, хэрэв
\[
(Y_{t_1},Y_{t_2},\ldots,Y_{t_n})
\] -ийн хамтарсан тархалт нь бүх бүхэл \(h\) болон
\[
t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_n
\]
хугацааны цэгүүдийн дурын олонлогийн хувьд
\[(Y_{t_1+h},Y_{t_2+h},\ldots,Y_{t_n+h})\]
-ийн хамтарсан тархалттай ижил байна.
Иймд процессийн магадлалын зан төлөв цаг хугацааны явцад өөрчлөгдөхгүй.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.3 Сул стационар байдал
Практикт сул стационар байдлыг илүү их ашигладаг.
Процесс нь дараах нөхцлүүд биелбэл сул стационар байна.

3.3.1 Дундаж
\[
E(Y_t)=\mu
\]
нь бүх \(t\)-ийн хувьд тогтмол.


3.3.2 Дисперс
\[
Var(Y_t)=\sigma^2
\]
нь бүх \(t\)-ийн хувьд тогтмол.


3.3.3 Ковариац
\[
Cov(Y_t,Y_{t-k})
\]
нь зөвхөн \(k\) хоцролтоос хамаарах бөгөөд \(t\) хугацаанаас хамаарахгүй.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.4 Автоковариацын функц
Автоковариацын функц нь
\[
\gamma(k)
=
Cov(Y_t,Y_{t-k}).
\]
Сул стационар процессийн хувьд
\[
\gamma(k)
\]
нь зөвхөн \(k\)-ээс хамаарна.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.5 Автокорреляцын функц
Автокорреляцын функц (ACF) нь
\[
\rho(k)
=
\frac{\gamma(k)}
     {\gamma(0)}.
\]
Учир нь
\[
\gamma(0)=Var(Y_t),
\]
ACF нь \(k\) хоцролтоор тусгаарлагдсан ажиглалтуудын хоорондын хамаарлыг хэмждэг.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.6 Цагаан чимээ нь стационар процесс
Цагаан чимээний процесс
\[
Y_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2)
\]
нь стационар, учир нь
\[
E(Y_t)=0,
\]
\[
Var(Y_t)=\sigma^2,
\]
ба
\[
Cov(Y_t,Y_{t-k})=0
\]
нь бүх \(k \neq 0\)-ийн хувьд биелнэ.
crumbs: 3  Стационар байдал

title: 3  Стационар байдал

3.8 Жишээ: Стационар бус цуваа
Санамсаргүй алхалтыг авч үзье:
\[

\]

\[
\varepsilon_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2).
\]

plot.ts(

  main = "Санамсаргүй алхалт",

Хувьсах байдал цаг хугацааны явцад нэмэгдэж, процесс тогтвортой дундажгүй байна.
Иймд санамсаргүй алхалт нь стационар бус байна.

title: 3  Стационар байдал
text:
3.10 Стационар байдал яагаад чухал вэ
Сонгодог таамаглах загваруудын ихэнх нь стационар байдлыг шаарддаг.

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.1 Introduction
The autocorrelation function (ACF) describes the dependence between observations separated by a given lag.
For a time series
\[
\{Y_t\},
\]
the ACF measures the strength of the linear relationship between
\[
Y_t
\]
and
\[
Y_{t-k}.
\]
The ACF is one of the most important tools in time series analysis.
It is widely used to:
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
identify serial dependence,
detect nonstationarity,
distinguish AR and MA models,
guide model selection.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.2 Autocovariance Function
For a weakly stationary process,
\[
\gamma(k)
=
Cov(Y_t,Y_{t-k})
\]
is called the autocovariance function.
Since
\[
Cov(Y_t,Y_{t-k})
=
E[(Y_t-\mu)(Y_{t-k}-\mu)],
\]
the autocovariance measures the dependence between observations separated by lag (k).

4.2.1 Properties
\[
\gamma(0)=Var(Y_t)
\]
and
\[
\gamma(k)=\gamma(-k).
\]
Thus the autocovariance function is symmetric.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.3 Definition of the ACF
The autocorrelation function is
\[
\rho(k)
=
\frac{\gamma(k)}
{\gamma(0)}.
\]
Since
\[
\gamma(0)=Var(Y_t),
\]
the ACF standardizes the covariance.
Therefore
\[
-1 \le \rho(k) \le 1.
\]

4.3.1 Important Values
At lag zero,
\[
\rho(0)=1.
\]
A value close to 1 indicates strong positive dependence.
A value close to -1 indicates strong negative dependence.
A value near 0 indicates little linear dependence.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.5 White Noise
Consider a white noise process
\[
Y_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Its autocorrelation function is
\[
\rho(0)=1,
\]
and
\[
\rho(k)=0,
\qquad k\ne0.
\]

4.5.1 Simulation

set.seed(123)

wn <- rnorm(200)

plot.ts(
  wn,
  main = "White Noise",
  ylab = expression(Y[t])
)










4.5.2 ACF Plot

acf(
  wn,
  main = "ACF of White Noise"
)








The sample autocorrelations fluctuate randomly around zero.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.6 AR(1) Process
Consider
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\]
where
\[
|\phi|<1.
\]
For an AR(1) process,
\[
\rho(k)=\phi^k.
\]
Thus the ACF decays geometrically.

4.6.1 Example

set.seed(123)

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.8),
  n=200
)

acf(
  ar1,
  main="ACF of AR(1)"
)








The autocorrelations decrease gradually as the lag increases.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.7 MA(1) Process
Consider
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]
The autocorrelation function is
\[
\rho(1)
=
\frac{\theta}
{1+\theta^2}
\]
and
\[
\rho(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]
Therefore the ACF cuts off after lag 1.

4.7.1 Example

set.seed(123)

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.5),
  n=200
)

acf(
  ma1,
  main="ACF of MA(1)"
)








Only the first lag tends to be significant.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.8 Interpretation of the ACF

4.8.1 White Noise

All autocorrelations are approximately zero.
No systematic dependence.



4.8.2 AR Process

Slow decay.
Correlations persist across lags.



4.8.3 MA Process

Sharp cutoff.
Dependence exists only for a limited number of lags.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.9 Statistical Significance
For a white noise process,
\[
SE(r_k)
\approx
\frac{1}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Approximate 95% bounds are
\[
\pm \frac{1.96}{\sqrt n}.
\]
For example, if
\[
n=200,
\]
then
\[
\pm\frac{1.96}{\sqrt{200}}
\approx
\pm0.139.
\]
Bars outside these bounds may indicate significant autocorrelation.
crumbs: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)

title: 4  The Autocorrelation Function (ACF)
text:
4.10 Example with Real Data

data(AirPassengers)

acf(
  AirPassengers,
  main="ACF of AirPassengers"
)








Observe the strong persistence and seasonality.

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.1 Оршил
Автокорреляцын функц (ACF) нь
\[
Y_t
\]
ба
\[
Y_{t-k}
\]
хоорондын корреляцийг хэмждэг.
Гэхдээ (k) хоцролт дээрх автокорреляц нь завсрын хоцролтуудаар дамжин шууд бус байдлаар нөлөөлөгдөж болно.
Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF) нь завсрын ажиглалтуудын
\[
Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2},\ldots,Y_{t-k+1}
\]
шугаман нөлөөг арилгасны дараа
\[
Y_t
\]
ба
\[
Y_{t-k}
\]
хоорондын шууд хамаарлыг хэмждэг.
PACF нь авторегрессив загваруудыг тодорхойлох хамгийн ашигтай хэрэгслүүдийн нэг юм.
crumbs: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.2 Motivation
Consider an AR(1) process
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t.
\]
Since
\[
Y_t
\]
depends directly only on
\[
Y_{t-1},
\]
any apparent correlation between
\[
Y_t
\]
and
\[
Y_{t-2}
\]
arises through
\[
Y_{t-1}.
\]
The PACF removes this indirect effect.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.3 Definition
The partial autocorrelation at lag (k), denoted by
\[
\alpha(k),
\]
is the correlation between
\[
Y_t
\]
and
\[
Y_{t-k}
\]
after controlling for
\[
Y_{t-1},Y_{t-2},\ldots,Y_{t-k+1}.
\]
Thus,
\[
\alpha(k)
\]
measures the direct contribution of lag (k).
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.4 Computing the PACF
In practice the PACF is estimated using recursive regression methods or the Yule-Walker equations.
Fortunately, R computes it automatically.

set.seed(123)

y <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.8),
  n=200
)

pacf(y)
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.5 PACF of White Noise
For white noise,
\[
Y_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2),
\]
there is no dependence between observations.
Therefore
\[
\alpha(k)=0,
\qquad k\ge1.
\]

5.5.1 Simulation

set.seed(123)

wn <- rnorm(200)

pacf(
  wn,
  main="PACF of White Noise"
)








All bars should fluctuate randomly around zero.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.6 PACF of an AR(1) Process
Consider
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\]
with
\[
|\phi|<1.
\]
The theoretical PACF is
\[
\alpha(1)=\phi,
\]
and
\[
\alpha(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]
Therefore, the PACF cuts off after lag 1.

5.6.1 Example

set.seed(123)

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.8),
  n=200
)

pacf(
  ar1,
  main="PACF of AR(1)"
)








A significant spike appears at lag 1, while later lags are close to zero.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.7 PACF of an AR(2) Process
Consider
\[
Y_t
=
0.7Y_{t-1}
-
0.3Y_{t-2}
+
\varepsilon_t.
\]

set.seed(123)

ar2 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=c(.7,-.3)),
  n=500
)

pacf(
  ar2,
  main="PACF of AR(2)"
)








The PACF exhibits significant values at lags 1 and 2 and then cuts off.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.8 PACF of an MA(1) Process
Consider
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]
Unlike an AR process, the PACF does not cut off.
Instead, it decreases gradually toward zero.

5.8.1 Example

set.seed(123)

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.5),
  n=200
)

pacf(
  ma1,
  main="PACF of MA(1)"
)








The PACF tails off rather than terminating abruptly.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.9 Comparison of ACF and PACF

5.9.1 AR Models
For an AR((p)) process:

ACF tails off.
PACF cuts off after lag (p).



5.9.2 MA Models
For an MA((q)) process:

ACF cuts off after lag (q).
PACF tails off.



5.9.3 ARMA Models
For an ARMA((p,q)) process:

ACF tails off.
PACF tails off.

Neither function exhibits a sharp cutoff.

5.11 Example: Comparing AR and MA Models

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

ar1 <- arima.sim(model=list(ar=.8), n=300)
acf(ar1, main="AR(1): ACF")
pacf(ar1, main="AR(1): PACF")

ma1 <- arima.sim(model=list(ma=.8), n=300)
acf(ma1, main="MA(1): ACF")
pacf(ma1, main="MA(1): PACF")








Observe:

AR(1): ACF tails off, PACF cuts off.
MA(1): ACF cuts off, PACF tails off.

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.12 Statistical Significance
For large samples,
\[
SE(r_k)
\approx
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
The PACF plot displays approximate 95% confidence limits
\[
\pm\frac{1.96}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Values outside these limits may indicate significant dependence.
crumbs: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)

title: 5  The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF)
text:
5.13 Summary

The PACF measures direct dependence at a given lag.
PACF removes the effect of intermediate observations.
AR((p)) processes have PACFs that cut off after lag (p).
MA((q)) processes have PACFs that tail off.
ACF and PACF together are the primary tools for model identification.

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.1 Introduction
The AR(1) model is the simplest and most important autoregressive model.
In an AR(1) process, the current observation depends on the immediately preceding observation and a random error.
The model serves as a foundation for understanding higher-order autoregressive models and many forecasting methods.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.2 Definition
An AR(1) process is defined by
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\]
where

\(\phi\) is the autoregressive parameter,
\(\varepsilon_t\sim WN(0,\sigma^2)\),
\(\{\varepsilon_t\}\) is a white noise process.

The parameter \(\phi\) determines the strength of dependence between consecutive observations.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.3 Stationarity Condition
The AR(1) process is stationary if
\[
|\phi|<1.
\]
If
\[
|\phi|\ge 1,
\]
the process is nonstationary.

6.3.1 Examples



Value of \(\phi\)
Interpretation




\(0\)
White noise


\(0.3\)
Weak dependence


\(0.8\)
Strong persistence


\(-0.8\)
Alternating behavior


\(1\)
Random walk (nonstationary)
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.4 Mean of an AR(1) Process
Taking expectations,
\[
E(Y_t)
=
\phi E(Y_{t-1}).
\]
Under stationarity,
\[
E(Y_t)=\mu.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mu=\phi\mu.
\]
Hence,
\[
\mu=0.
\]
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.5 Variance of an AR(1) Process
Since
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\]
the stationary variance is
\[
Var(Y_t)
=
\frac{\sigma^2}
     {1-\phi^2}.
\]
As \(|\phi|\) approaches 1, the variance increases.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.6 Autocovariance Function
For a stationary AR(1) process,
\[
\gamma(k)
=
\phi^{k}\gamma(0).
\]
Since
\[
\gamma(0)
=
\frac{\sigma^2}
     {1-\phi^2},
\]
all autocovariances are determined by \(\phi\).
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.7 Autocorrelation Function
The ACF of an AR(1) process is
\[
\rho(k)=\phi^k.
\]
This is one of the most important results in time series analysis.

6.7.1 Consequences
If
\[
\phi=0.8,
\]
then
\[
\rho(1)=0.8,
\]
\[
\rho(2)=0.64,
\]
\[
\rho(3)=0.512.
\]
Thus the ACF decreases gradually toward zero.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.8 Partial Autocorrelation Function
For an AR(1) process,
\[
PACF(1)=\phi,
\]
and
\[
PACF(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]
Therefore the PACF cuts off after lag 1.
This property is widely used to identify AR(1) models.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.9 Simulation

6.9.1 Positive Dependence

set.seed(123)

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model = list(ar = 0.8),
  n = 200
)

plot.ts(
  ar1,
  main = expression(AR(1)~with~phi==0.8),
  ylab = expression(Y[t])
)








Observe the persistence of consecutive observations.


6.9.2 Negative Dependence

set.seed(123)

ar1neg <- arima.sim(
  model = list(ar = -0.8),
  n = 200
)

plot.ts(
  ar1neg,
  main = expression(AR(1)~with~phi==-0.8),
  ylab = expression(Y[t])
)








Successive observations tend to alternate in sign.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.10 ACF of an AR(1) Process

acf(
  ar1,
  main="ACF of AR(1)"
)








The ACF decays geometrically.
This tailing-off behavior is characteristic of autoregressive processes.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.11 PACF of an AR(1) Process

pacf(
  ar1,
  main="PACF of AR(1)"
)








Only the first lag should be significant.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.12 Lag Plot
A lag plot reveals the dependence between \(Y_t\) and \(Y_{t-1}\).

plot(
  x = ar1[-length(ar1)],
  y = ar1[-1],
  xlab = expression(Y[t-1]),
  ylab = expression(Y[t]),
  pch = 16
)








A positive linear pattern should be visible.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.13 Comparison of Different Values of \(\phi\)

par(mfrow=c(2,2))

plot.ts(
  arima.sim(model=list(ar=.2), n=200),
  main=expression(phi==0.2)
)

plot.ts(
  arima.sim(model=list(ar=.5), n=200),
  main=expression(phi==0.5)
)

plot.ts(
  arima.sim(model=list(ar=.8), n=200),
  main=expression(phi==0.8)
)

plot.ts(
  arima.sim(model=list(ar=-0.8), n=200),
  main=expression(phi==-0.8)
)








Observe how the degree of dependence changes as \(\phi\) changes.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.14 Parameter Estimation
An AR(1) model can be estimated using maximum likelihood.

fit <- arima(
  ar1,
  order=c(1,0,0)
)

fit


Call:
arima(x = ar1, order = c(1, 0, 0))

Coefficients:
         ar1  intercept
      0.7235    -0.0239
s.e.  0.0491     0.2363

sigma^2 estimated as 0.8744:  log likelihood = -270.73,  aic = 547.46


The estimated value of \(\phi\) should be close to the true value used in simulation.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.15 Forecasting
For an AR(1) model,
\[
\hat{Y}_{t+1}
=
\phi Y_t.
\]
More generally,
\[
\hat{Y}_{t+h}
=
\phi^h Y_t.
\]
As \(h\) increases,
\[
\phi^h \rightarrow 0,
\]
and forecasts approach the mean of the process.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.16 Interpretation

6.16.1 Positive \(\phi\)
If
\[
\phi>0,
\]
large values tend to follow large values and small values tend to follow small values.


6.16.2 Negative \(\phi\)
If
\[
\phi<0,
\]
successive observations tend to move in opposite directions.


6.16.3 Near Zero
If
\[
\phi\approx 0,
\]
the process resembles white noise.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:
6.17 Summary
The AR(1) process
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t
\]
is the simplest autoregressive model.
Key properties:

Stationary when \(|\phi|<1\).
Mean equals zero.
Variance equals \(\frac{\sigma^2}{1-\phi^2}\).
ACF: \(\rho(k)=\phi^k\).
PACF cuts off after lag 1.

These characteristics make AR(1) a fundamental model in time series analysis.
crumbs: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)

title: 6  The Autoregressive Process of Order One: AR(1)
text:

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.1 Introduction
The MA(1) model is the simplest moving average process.
Unlike an autoregressive model, an MA(1) process does not depend directly on past observations. Instead, it depends on the current and previous random shocks.
The MA(1) model is fundamental in time series analysis and serves as a building block for higher-order MA and ARMA models.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.2 Definition
An MA(1) process is defined by
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1},
\]
where

({_t}) is a white noise process,
(E(_t)=0),
(Var(_t)=^2),
() is the moving average parameter.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.3 Mean
Taking expectations,
\[
E(Y_t)
=
E(\varepsilon_t)
+
\theta E(\varepsilon_{t-1}).
\]
Since
\[
E(\varepsilon_t)=0,
\]
it follows that
\[
E(Y_t)=0.
\]
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.4 Variance
Since the white noise terms are uncorrelated,
\[
Var(Y_t)
=
Var(\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}),
\]
which gives
\[
Var(Y_t)
=
(1+\theta^2)\sigma^2.
\]
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.5 Autocovariance Function

7.5.1 Lag 0
\[
\gamma(0)
=
(1+\theta^2)\sigma^2.
\]


7.5.2 Lag 1
\[
\gamma(1)
=
\theta\sigma^2.
\]


7.5.3 Lag (k>1)
\[
\gamma(k)=0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\gamma(k)=
\begin{cases}
(1+\theta^2)\sigma^2, & k=0,\\
\theta\sigma^2, & k=1,\\
0, & k>1.
\end{cases}
\]
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.6 Autocorrelation Function
Dividing by ((0)),
\[
\rho(1)
=
\frac{\theta}
     {1+\theta^2},
\]
and
\[
\rho(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]
This is the most important property of an MA(1) process.
The ACF cuts off after lag 1.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.7 Example
If
\[
\theta=0.5,
\]
then
\[
\rho(1)
=
\frac{0.5}{1+0.25}
=
0.40.
\]
If
\[
\theta=0.2,
\]
then
\[
\rho(1)
=
\frac{0.2}{1.04}
\approx 0.192.
\]
This value should appear in the sample ACF.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.8 Invertibility
For an MA(1) model,
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1},
\]
invertibility requires
\[
|\theta|<1.
\]
Invertibility ensures a unique representation of the process.
This condition plays a role similar to the stationarity condition
\[
|\phi|<1
\]
for AR models.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.9 Simulation

7.9.1 MA(1) with ()

set.seed(123)

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.5),
  n=200
)

plot.ts(
  ma1,
  main=expression(MA(1)~with~theta==0.5),
  ylab=expression(Y[t])
)










7.9.2 MA(1) with ()

set.seed(123)

ma1neg <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=-.5),
  n=200
)

plot.ts(
  ma1neg,
  main=expression(MA(1)~with~theta==-0.5),
  ylab=expression(Y[t])
)
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.10 ACF of an MA(1) Process

acf(
  ma1,
  main="ACF of MA(1)"
)








Observe:

Significant spike at lag 1.
Near-zero autocorrelations for lags greater than 1.

This cutoff behavior is the hallmark of an MA(1) process.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.11 PACF of an MA(1) Process

pacf(
  ma1,
  main="PACF of MA(1)"
)








Unlike the ACF, the PACF does not cut off.
Instead, it decreases gradually toward zero.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.12 Lag-1 Scatter Plot
The relationship between
\[
Y_t
\]
and
\[
Y_{t-1}
\]
may be examined using a lag plot.

plot(
  x = ma1[-length(ma1)],
  y = ma1[-1],
  xlab = expression(Y[t-1]),
  ylab = expression(Y[t]),
  pch = 16
)








For positive (), the plot tends to exhibit a weak positive linear pattern.
For negative (), the pattern slopes downward.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.13 Lag-2 Scatter Plot
Consider
\[
(Y_{t-2},Y_t).
\]

plot(
  x = ma1[-c(length(ma1)-1,length(ma1))],
  y = ma1[-c(1,2)],
  xlab = expression(Y[t-2]),
  ylab = expression(Y[t]),
  pch = 16
)








Since
\[
\rho(2)=0,
\]
the points should display little or no linear pattern.
The scatter plot generally resembles a random cloud.
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

text:

text:
7.15 Estimation
An MA(1) model can be estimated using maximum likelihood.

fit <- arima(
  ma1,
  order=c(0,0,1)

fit

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.16 Example: ()

set.seed(123)

ma1.2 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.2),
  n=500

acf(ma1.2)








The theoretical lag-1 autocorrelation is

\]

crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.17 Forecasting
For an MA(1) process,
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1},
\]
the one-step-ahead forecast depends on the most recent estimated shock.
For horizons greater than one,
\[
\hat Y_{t+h}
\]
rapidly converges to the mean of the process.
Since the mean is zero,
\[
\hat Y_{t+h}
\rightarrow 0.
\]
crumbs: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)

title: 7  The Moving Average Process of Order One: MA(1)
text:
7.18 Summary
The MA(1) process
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}
\]
has the following properties:

Mean:

\[
E(Y_t)=0.
\]

Variance:

\[
Var(Y_t)
=
(1+\theta^2)\sigma^2.
\]

ACF:

\[
\rho(1)
=
\frac{\theta}{1+\theta^2},
\]
\[
\rho(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]

PACF tails off gradually.
Invertibility requires

\[
|\theta|<1.
\]
The ACF cutoff at lag 1 is the most important identifying characteristic of an MA(1) process.

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.1 Introduction
The ARMA model combines the ideas of autoregressive (AR) and moving average (MA) processes.
It is one of the most important classes of stationary time series models and forms the foundation of the Box-Jenkins methodology.
An ARMA model can capture both:
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
persistence through past observations,
short-term dependence through past shocks.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.2 Definition
An ARMA((p,q)) process is defined by
\[
Y_t
=
\phi_1Y_{t-1}
+\phi_2Y_{t-2}
+\cdots
+\phi_pY_{t-p}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1}
+\theta_2\varepsilon_{t-2}
+\cdots
+\theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q},
\]
where
\[
\{\varepsilon_t\}
\sim
WN(0,\sigma^2).
\]
Here:

(p) = autoregressive order,
(q) = moving average order.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.3 Special Cases

8.3.1 AR Model
If
\[
q=0,
\]
then
\[
ARMA(p,0)=AR(p).
\]


8.3.2 MA Model
If
\[
p=0,
\]
then
\[
ARMA(0,q)=MA(q).
\]
Thus AR and MA processes are special cases of the ARMA model.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.4 The ARMA(1,1) Model
The simplest ARMA model is
\[
Y_t
=
\phi Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]
This model combines:

the dependence structure of AR(1),
the shock structure of MA(1).
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.5 Stationarity
For ARMA processes, stationarity depends on the AR part.
For ARMA(1,1),
\[
|\phi|<1
\]
is required for stationarity.

8.5.1 Examples



()
Stationary?




0.3
Yes


0.8
Yes


-0.5
Yes


1.0
No


1.1
No
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.6 Invertibility
Invertibility depends on the MA part.
For ARMA(1,1),
\[
|\theta|<1
\]
is required for invertibility.
This ensures a unique representation of the process.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.7 Mean
For a stationary ARMA(1,1),
\[
E(Y_t)=0.
\]
More generally, if a constant term is included, the mean is constant over time.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.8 Simulation of ARMA(1,1)
Consider
\[
Y_t
=
0.7Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
0.4\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]

set.seed(123)

arma11 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7, ma=.4),
  n=300
)

plot.ts(
  arma11,
  main="ARMA(1,1) Process",
  ylab=expression(Y[t])
)








Observe the persistence created by the AR component and the short-term effects created by the MA component.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.9 ACF of an ARMA Process

acf(
  arma11,
  main="ACF of ARMA(1,1)"
)








Unlike MA models, the ACF does not cut off.
Unlike pure AR models, the pattern is often more complex.
The ACF generally tails off toward zero.
crumbs: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.10 PACF of an ARMA Process

pacf(
  arma11,
  main="PACF of ARMA(1,1)"
)








The PACF also tails off.
This is one of the identifying characteristics of ARMA models.

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.11 Model Identification

8.11.1 AR(p)

ACF tails off.
PACF cuts off.



8.11.2 MA(q)

ACF cuts off.
PACF tails off.



8.11.3 ARMA(p,q)

ACF tails off.
PACF tails off.

Therefore ARMA models are usually identified by examining both functions simultaneously.

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.12 Comparing AR(1), MA(1), and ARMA(1,1)

par(mfrow=c(3,2))

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7),
  n=300
)

acf(ar1, main="AR(1): ACF")
pacf(ar1, main="AR(1): PACF")

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.7),
  n=300
)

acf(ma1, main="MA(1): ACF")
pacf(ma1, main="MA(1): PACF")

arma11 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.7, ma=.4),
  n=300
)

acf(arma11, main="ARMA(1,1): ACF")
pacf(arma11, main="ARMA(1,1): PACF")








Compare the characteristic patterns.

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.13 Lag Plot
A lag plot may be used to visualize dependence.

plot(
  x = arma11[-length(arma11)],
  y = arma11[-1],
  xlab = expression(Y[t-1]),
  ylab = expression(Y[t]),

The relationship is generally stronger than white noise and reflects both AR and MA effects.

8.15 Model Selection Using AIC
Different ARMA models can be compared using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).

fit1 <- arima(arma11, order=c(1,0,0))
fit2 <- arima(arma11, order=c(0,0,1))
fit3 <- arima(arma11, order=c(1,0,1))

AIC(fit1, fit2, fit3)

fit1  3 890.8641
fit2  3 976.2085
fit3  4 869.2151


The model with the smallest AIC is usually preferred.

title: 8  The Autoregressive Moving Average Process: ARMA
text:
8.17 Summary
An ARMA((p,q)) model combines:

autoregressive dependence,
moving average dependence.

For ARMA(1,1),
\[
Y_t
=
\phi Y_{t-1}
+
\varepsilon_t
+
\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]
Important properties:

Stationarity depends on the AR component.
Invertibility depends on the MA component.
ACF tails off.
PACF tails off.
Widely used for stationary time series.

ARMA models provide a flexible framework for describing many real-world time series.

5.2 Урам зориг
AR(1) процессыг авч үзье:
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t.
\]
Учир нь
\[
Y_t

зөвхөн
\[

\]
-ээс шууд хамаардаг тул
\[
Y_t
\]
ба
\[
Y_{t-2}
\]
хоорондын аливаа илэрхий корреляц нь
\[

\]

5.3 Тодорхойлолт
(k) хоцролт дээрх хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцыг
\[
\alpha(k)
\]
гэж тэмдэглэх бөгөөд энэ нь
\[

-ийг хянасны дараа

Y_t

Y_{t-k}

хоорондын корреляц юм.

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.5 Цагаан чимээний PACF
Цагаан чимээний хувьд
\[
Y_t \sim WN(0,\sigma^2),
\]
ажиглалтуудын хооронд хамаарал байхгүй.
Иймд
\[
\alpha(k)=0,
\qquad k\ge1.
\]

5.5.1 Симуляц

set.seed(123)

wn <- rnorm(200)

pacf(
  wn,
  main="Цагаан чимээний PACF"
)








Бүх баганууд тэг орчимд санамсаргүйгээр хэлбэлзэх ёстой.

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.6 AR(1) процессын PACF
Дараахьыг авч үзье:
\[
Y_t=\phi Y_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t,
\]
энд
\[
|\phi|<1.
\]
Онолын PACF нь
\[
\alpha(1)=\phi,
\]
ба
\[
\alpha(k)=0,
\qquad k>1.
\]
Иймд PACF нь 1 хоцролтын дараа тасардаг.

5.6.1 Жишээ

set.seed(123)

ar1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=.8),
  n=200
)

pacf(
  ar1,
  main="AR(1)-ийн PACF"
)








1 хоцролт дээр ач холбогдолтой оргил гарч, дараагийн хоцролтууд тэгтэй ойрхон байна.
crumbs: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.7 AR(2) процессын PACF
Дараахьыг авч үзье:
\[
Y_t
=
0.7Y_{t-1}
-
0.3Y_{t-2}
+
\varepsilon_t.
\]

ar2 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ar=c(.7,-.3)),
  n=500
)

pacf(
  ar2,
  main="AR(2)-ын PACF"
)








PACF нь 1 ба 2 хоцролтууд дээр ач холбогдолтой утгуудыг харуулсны дараа тасардаг.

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.8 MA(1) процессын PACF
Дараахьыг авч үзье:
\[
Y_t=\varepsilon_t+\theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.
\]
AR процессоос ялгаатай нь PACF тасардаггүй.
Харин аажмаар тэг рүү буурдаг.

ma1 <- arima.sim(
  model=list(ma=.5),
  n=200
)

pacf(
  ma1,
  main="MA(1)-ийн PACF"
)








PACF огцом зогсохын оронд аажмаар буурдаг.

text:
5.12 Статистик ач холбогдол
Том түүврийн хувьд
\[
SE(r_k)
\approx
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
PACF график нь ойролцоогоор 95% итгэлцлийн хязгаарыг харуулдаг:
\[
\pm\frac{1.96}{\sqrt n}.
\]
Эдгээр хязгаараас гадуур байгаа утгууд нь ач холбогдолтой хамаарлыг илтгэж болно.

title: 5  Хэсэгчилсэн автокорреляцын функц (PACF)
text:
5.13 Дүгнэлт

PACF нь өгөгдсөн хоцролт дээрх шууд хамаарлыг хэмждэг.
PACF нь завсрын ажиглалтуудын нөлөөг арилгадаг.
AR((p)) процессуудын PACF нь (p) хоцролтын дараа тасардаг.
MA((q)) процессуудын PACF нь аажмаар буурдаг.
ACF ба PACF хамтдаа загвар тодорхойлох үндсэн хэрэгсэл болдог.
